title: A fruit-eating oviraptorosaur from the Late Cretaceous
institution: Royal Ontario Museum · Stony Brook University
summary: A new oviraptorosaur from the Late Cretaceous preserves jaw musculature interpreted as specialised for fruit eating — an unusual diet for a theropod whose relatives were mostly carnivorous or omnivorous. The authors describe the genus Infernogallus and compare its chewing apparatus with living fruit-eating birds.

title: A new dicynodont from Tanzania and the age of the earliest dinosaurs
summary: A new species of the plant-eating synapsid Dinodontosaurus is described from the Manda Beds. Its anatomy supports a younger age for the beds than previously argued, which affects the dating of the fragmentary fossils once claimed to be among the oldest dinosaurs. A reminder that MESOZO's scope is prehistoric life, not dinosaurs alone.

title: A new nodosaurid ankylosaur from Hokkaido
summary: CT scanning of cranial material collected more than two decades ago revealed a new nodosaurid genus and species. The study reconstructs previously hidden jaw and inner-ear anatomy and places the animal among Asian nodosaurids, with implications for dispersal along coastal routes.

title: A large troodontid from the Kirtland Formation
institution: New Mexico Museum of Natural History & Science
summary: A bone found in 2005 in the Kirtland Formation is described as a new genus of troodontid. At an estimated 2.4–3 m in length and 70–140 kg, it is one of the largest troodontids known, expanding the size range of a group usually represented by small, bird-like dinosaurs.

title: A new mamenchisaurid sauropod from northeastern Thailand
summary: A new long-necked sauropod from the Upper Jurassic Phu Kradung Formation is the first mamenchisaurid named from Thailand. The find strengthens the case that this predominantly East Asian sauropod family ranged more widely across Southeast Asia than previously thought.

title: A four-winged microraptorine from the Changma Basin
institution: Field Museum · Carnegie Museum of Natural History
summary: A single non-avian dinosaur specimen from a fossil bed otherwise dominated by early birds is described as a new microraptorine. Its long feathers on both forelimbs and hindlimbs suggest a gliding animal, and its size and carnivorous dentition make it a candidate predator of the early birds preserved alongside it.
